transcript.content: Hello, welcome in. I'm Dr. Smith. What brings you in to see me today?

Well… I suppose I’ve just been feeling like I’m always on the go. Even on quiet days, I’ll start with the garden club list, then I’m in my knitting bag, then I’m sorting travel papers… and somehow I haven’t really finished any of it.
During these periods when you're jumping from task to task, do you also notice your mood feeling unusually high, elated, or irritable, more than what's normal for you?
I don’t think so. I mean… I get a bit frustrated with myself sometimes, but not unusually happy or anything like that.

Would you say this difficulty staying focused and jumping between tasks has been part of how you've always been, even back in school or early adulthood, or is this something that's developed more recently?

I think it’s been around a long time. Even in grade school, teachers would tell my mother I was bright but… scattered. Losing papers, talking when I shouldn’t, fidgeting before I finished my work. That sort of thing.

latest_inference.note: Chronic, lifelong pattern of distractibility, fidgeting, and impulsivity since childhood, without episodes of elevated/irritable mood, argues against bipolar/hypomanic disorder. No anxiety symptoms or physical signs of thyroid dysfunction reported, reducing likelihood of F41.1 and E05.9. This strongly supports a primary diagnosis of ADHD.

final_diagnosis.reason: Patient reports a lifelong pattern (since grade school) of inattentiveness, disorganization, distractibility, and impulsive fidgeting/talking, without episodic mood elevation or irritability that would suggest a manic or hypomanic episode. Symptoms are chronic and pervasive rather than episodic, consistent with Attention-Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder, predominantly inattentive presentation (F90.0), rather than a mood disorder such as Bipolar Disorder (F31.9) which was explicitly ruled out by absence of elevated/irritable mood episodes. Combined type (F90.2) considered but hyperactive-impulsive symptoms were less prominent than inattentive symptoms in current description.
